TEMPERATURE OF ROCKET ENGINE COOLING CHANNELS 17

is demonstrated in Figure 4a, where the coolant bulk temperature is presented for the
case of k ¼ 8 and for various grid refinements. Note, that the result relevant to the
selected grid (see solid line) differs from the extrapolated exact solution less than
0.45%.
The quasi-2-D model solution approximates the CFD solution in a better way
in the case of high aspect ratio; in fact, the temperature increase of the two models
differs by more than 29% in the case of k ¼ 1 and only by 1.2% in the case of k ¼ 8
(Figure 1b). The good match of the quasi-2-D model with the reference CFD solution in the case of high aspect ratio is due to the physical and mathematical formulation of the simplified model. In fact, the heat transfer and the skin friction force are
carefully modeled along the lateral walls, whereas their evaluation on the channel
bases (Eqs. (28) and (29) for the heat transfer, and Eq. (10) for the skin friction)
is based on a less accurate 1-D approach. As a consequence, in the case of low aspect
ratio, where a relevant portion of the channel perimeter is given by channel bases, the
prediction is less accurate than in the case of high aspect ratio, where the contribution of the channel bases to the heat transfer and skin friction is almost negligible.
Note also that the quasi-2-D temperature of k ¼ 8 is close to the CFD solution along
the whole channel length, while in the case of low aspect ratio the quasi-2-D and the
CFD bulk temperatures difference increases along the channel. The different behavior between low and high aspect ratio is confirmed also by the bulk pressure behavior, which is shown in Figure 4c for the case of k ¼ 1 and in Figure 4d for the case of
k ¼ 8. The pressure drop difference between the two models is 18.8% in the former
case and 4.4% in the latter. In particular, the quasi-2-D model overestimates the
coolant pressure loss in the case of low aspect ratio, while in Figure 4d the quasi-2-D
pressure crosses the CFD solution. The comparison of fluid temperature growth and
pressure drop obtained by the quasi-2-D and the CFD computations is reported in
Table 2. Results show that good agreement is obtained in the case of HARCC.

To better evaluate the capability of the proposed model to reproduce the cooling channel flow, the comparison against the CFD solution has also been performed
with respect to the radial direction (Figure 5). Note that to compare quasi-2-D and
the CFD solutions, the 3-D data have been reduced to a 2-D form by averaging the
CFD solution along direction z. The velocity profile in the radial direction is characterized by a peak value, located in the lower part of the channel height, which is
due to the lower inertia of the higher temperature fluid in that region; the temperature profile is characterized by an evident stratification for both aspect ratios. Of
course, the radial behavior can only be approximately reproduced by the quasi-2-D
model, because the CFD model describes the cinematic and thermal boundary layers
